references.text: Micah summarizes what the Lord requires: to do justice, love mercy (ἔλεος), and walk humbly with God – the same principle Jesus points to when he says "go and do likewise".
Hosea conveys that God desires mercy (chesed/ἔλεος) and not sacrifice, emphasizing the same principle of mercy that Jesus highlights in the parable of the good Samaritan.
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy" – this corresponds with the call to show ἔλεος (mercy) in Luke 10:37.
Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 and says "I desire mercy, not sacrifice", which supports the central message of the parable of the good Samaritan.

The second greatest commandment – "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" – is the command that the entire parable of the good Samaritan illustrates, and to which Jesus' call "go and do likewise" points back.
Jesus says "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful" – a direct parallel to the call to show mercy as the Samaritan did.

The initial dialogue between the expert in the law and Jesus about inheriting eternal life and loving one's neighbor provides the context that the parable and the call "go and do likewise" respond to.
James writes that judgment is without mercy toward anyone who has shown no mercy, but mercy triumphs over judgment – this underscores the importance of acting like the good Samaritan.

John writes that whoever sees a brother in need and shuts their heart against him does not have God's love in them – a practical application of the same principle Jesus conveys with "go and do likewise".
Paul urges us to do good to everyone, reflecting Jesus' universal call to boundless mercy, as demonstrated by the Samaritan toward a stranger.
